content: The evaluation of additional serological markers, such as hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg), is essential for understanding the status of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Measurement of aminotransferase levels, including alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), provides insight into the degree of liver inflammation. Quantification of HBV DNA levels is critical for assessing viral replication and disease progression. Non-invasive methods, such as the AST-to-platelet ratio index (APRI), transient elastography (FibroScan®), or FibroTest, are used to determine the stage of liver fibrosis. A comprehensive clinical evaluation should include assessment for signs of cirrhosis, evidence of hepatic decompensation, and measurement of serum bilirubin, albumin, ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, prothrombin time, and a complete blood count, including platelet count. Routine investigations for individuals with HBV include ultrasonography and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) measurement for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance, as well as endoscopy to screen for esophageal varices in those with cirrhosis. A history of HBV infection is indicated by the presence of antibodies such as anti-HBs and anti-HBc, while immunity following vaccination is characterized by the presence of anti-HBs alone. Recently, quantification of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) has been proposed as a prognostic marker and for monitoring treatment response. Detection of HBV DNA remains the gold standard for quantifying viremia and monitoring viral replication during antiviral therapy. Serum HBV DNA concentrations, measured using real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR), correlate with disease progression and help differentiate HBeAg-negative infection from HBeAg-negative disease. WHO standards recommend expressing HBV DNA levels in international units per milliliter (IU/mL) for consistency. Aminotransferase levels can fluctuate over time, and single measurements of ALT and AST are insufficient to determine disease stage. Typically, ALT levels are higher than AST levels, but as the disease progresses to cirrhosis, the AST/ALT ratio may reverse. Tests of liver synthetic function and portal hypertension include serum albumin, bilirubin, platelet count, and prothrombin time. Liver biopsy, historically used to assess necroinflammation and fibrosis, has largely been replaced by validated non-invasive methods in adults with chronic hepatitis B (CHB). These methods include blood and serum fibrosis markers, such as APRI and FIB-4, as well as commercial tests like FibroTest and transient elastography (FibroScan®). The degree of hepatic fibrosis is a key determinant of prognosis, while HBV activity may vary over time. Quantitative HBsAg levels are highest in HBeAg-positive individuals but can also be elevated in those with anti-HBe-positive infection. However, in HBeAg-negative individuals, HBsAg is predominantly expressed from integrated viral genomes and correlates weakly with intrahepatic covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA). HBsAg concentrations vary by genotype, and low levels (<1000 IU/mL) in HBeAg-negative individuals with HBV DNA <2000 IU/mL and normal aminotransferase levels are associated with improved outcomes. Transition to HBeAg-negative inactive infection, accompanied by reduced cccDNA transcriptional activity, lowers the risk of adverse outcomes. Emerging biomarkers, such as core-related antigen (HBcrAg) and hepatitis B RNA (HBV RNA), may improve risk stratification by reflecting the size and transcriptional activity of the cccDNA pool. However, these biomarkers remain research tools, as commercial assays are not yet available. People with hepatitis B often face barriers to accessing care and treatment, including limited availability of diagnostics, reliance on hospital-based specialist care, and out-of-pocket expenses. Adherence to antiviral therapy is frequently suboptimal, with high rates of loss to follow-up. Provider training is crucial to reduce stigma, dispel misinformation, and effectively communicate the importance of disease management and ongoing monitoring. Stigma and discrimination associated with hepatitis B can lead to social exclusion, relationship instability, and difficulties in accessing employment or education. Discrimination may also result in restrictions on migration, deportation, or denial of opportunities to serve in the military or police forces. Understanding the lived experiences of stigma and discrimination is essential to address their impact on healthcare utilization and outcomes. Antiviral therapy with nucleos(t)ide analogues has been shown to delay cirrhosis progression, reduce HCC incidence, and improve long-term survival. Most patients require long-term, potentially lifelong, therapy. Current antiviral drugs, such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), entecavir (ETV), and tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF), are highly potent against HBV and have a high barrier to resistance. Research is ongoing to develop curative therapies that eliminate all replicative forms of HBV, including cccDNA, thereby reducing the need for lifelong treatment. Curative strategies include agents targeting infected cells and immunotherapeutic approaches to enhance HBV-specific adaptive immune responses or activate innate intrahepatic immunity. Investigational treatments include entry inhibitors, RNA interference agents (e.g., small interfering RNA [siRNA]), capsid assembly modulators, and immunomodulatory approaches. However, progress in identifying optimal combinations of novel antivirals and immunomodulators to achieve functional cure has been slow. Management considerations for specific populations, such as those co-infected with HIV, HDV, or HCV, pregnant women, children, adolescents, and healthcare workers, are addressed in dedicated guidelines. The WHO has developed updated recommendations for hepatitis B testing, care, and treatment using the GRADE approach to evidence review. Systematic reviews, cost-effectiveness analyses, and surveys of values and preferences have informed these guidelines, with a focus on lowand middle-income countries. The guidelines emphasize patient-centered care and the importance of addressing stigma and discrimination to improve health outcomes.
